caseno: CIVIL PETITION FOR LEAVE TO APPEAL. NO. 64 OF 2003
lawyer:
For the Petitioner: Mr. Mahbubey Alam, Senior. Advocate. Instructed by Mr. Chowdhury Md. Zahangir. Advocate-on-record.
Respondents: Not represented.
parties:
Mrs. Arati Deb ------ Petitioner

full_judgment:
Mr. Mohammad Fazlul Karim, J.:- The petitioner mother of detenu Suvro Deb. seeks leave to appeal against the impugned judgment and order dated 6.1.2003 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.7871 of 2002 discharging the rule maintaining the order of detention dated 10.12.2002 passed by the respondent no.3 issued under Memo contained in Miscellaneous Case No.2978 of 2002 under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, 1947. 

 2. The petitioner tiled the writ petition on 14.12.2002 challenging the said order of detention of the detenu Suvro Dev stating, inter alia, in the writ petition that the parents of the detenu are retired teachers the father being a retired Headmaster of Government High Scholl and the mother a retired teacher of Ram Krishna Girls' Primary School. Challibondar, Sylhet and the detenu is an Honour's Graduate in Biochemistry form Dhaka University and a talented musician and participated in several musical programs organized by freedom lighters even while he child staying in India. The detenu is a peace loving, honest and patriot and he never involved himself in any activities causing insecurity either of the State or of the society and being an artist engaged in spreading the message of peace for the society through his devotional and patriotic songs. The detenu was arrested by the police on 5.12.2002 in connection with Ramna P.S. Case NO.16 dated 4.12.2002 under sections 467/468/471 /4 19/ 420/109 of the Penal Code and was produced before the Metropolitan magistrate. Dhaka on 6.12.2002; police prayed remand for 5 days and the Metropolitan Magistrate. Dhaka rejected the prayer for remand for 5 days and the Metropolitan Magistrate, Dhaka rejected the prayer for remand and he was sent to jail. The initial order of detention was passed in Miscellaneous case No. 2978/2002 dated 10.12.2002 by the respondent No.3 for detention of the detenu for a period of 30 days under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 and same was served upon the detenu in Dhaka Central Jail on 11.12.2002. 

 3. The petitioner upon receipt of the grounds of detention served on 21.12.2002 tiled an supplementary affidavit denying all the allegations made in the grounds of detention against the detenu namely that he is an associate of top terrorist Kala Farook or that he is directly or indirectly involved in sending important information and papers out of the country or that he is involved in creating opportunity for Kala Farooq to leave the country or that he is involved in deep conspiracy taking part in various subversive activities and thereby damaging the image of the country or that if he is allowed to remain free he may create disturbance indulging in terrorist activities and can also illegally send outside some important information of the State or upon his arrest on 4.12.2002 he made an statement to the effect that Kala Farooq had illegal arms or that neither in case No.2 dated 4.11.2002 or in any other cases the detenu made any statement to the effect that Kala Farooq had any illegal arms or that he prayed for any permission from the Ministry of Cultural Affairs for Kala Farooq for the purpose of trafficking him abroad or that he created papers as leader of the cultural team or that he gave certificate to Kala Farooq Showing him as an artist or that in collusion with Abdur Rashid alias Kala Farooq and Nazrul Islam Koraishi lie created forged and fraudulent document to give opportunity to kala Farooq to go abroad or that he built up a secret network with the help of the terrorist for transferring secret information out of the country or that he is creating communal disturbances or that he is involved in damaging communal harmony and peace or that he is involved in activities in a disguise of the polite artist or that he is creating law and order situation and thereby damaging the image of the country abroad or that he is a professional and habitual cheat and arms cadre or that he is involved for a long time in terrorist activities including holding communal riots or that for the aforesaid activities the law and order situation has deteriorated and image of the country has been damaged or that due to his activities the law and order situation in Ramna area of Dhaka City has seriously been affected and deteriorated or that law and order and public peace will be under threat if the detenu is allowed to remain free or that the offence committed by him is attracted tinder section 2(f) (iii) of the Special Powers Act or that it is necessary to detain him under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act, terming those allegations as false, concocted and malafide. The petitioner further stated that the detenu was never involved in any illegal activities and he never co-operated with kala Farooq for leaving the country. The detenu is a renowned artist of the country and he has visited several countries of the world as a member of the Cultural team and on many occasions he lead the cultural team as its leader and due to his excellent performance the fame of the country has been enhanced and Bangladesh is being treated as a modern country with rich cultural background and that already a criminal case has been started in Ramna P.S. being Case No. 16(12) 2002 under section 476/468/471/ 419/420 and 109 of the Penal Code against the detenu on 4.12.2002 and he has been arrested in the said case on 5.12.2002. and the Magistrate allowed the prayer of the Police for his remand on 8.12.2002. Challenging the said order of remand the detenu has filed an application before the High Court Division under section 439 read with section 498 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Rule has been issued in the said application on 18.12.2002 and the detenu has been enlarged on bail by the High Court Division. The ground of detention are vague, indefinite and has nothing to prejudice the security of Bangladesh or to endanger public safety or the detenu has not doile nothing for hampering maintenance of public order and thus prayed for declaring the order of detention of the detenu to have been passed without lawful authority. 

 6. The detenu was detained under section 3(2) of the Special Powers Act by the District Magistrate pursuant to memo dated 10.12.2002 served on the detenu on 11.12.2002 while in custody in connection with a criminal case and the grounds of detention have been served on the detenu on 21.12.2002. the said grounds of detention stated, inter alia, as under: 

 8. The object of supplying the grounds detailed above are not only for the detenu to enable him to make an effective representation before the Advisory Board constituted under the Special Powers Act but also for placing the same for the consideration of the High Court Division to see the application of the mind of the detaining authority in case these are challenged. Although the satisfaction of the detaining authority is the subjective one but the Court would see as to whether there is some material before the detaining authority to from an opinion as to the necessity of an order of detention. 

 9. In the case of Rameswar Lal Patewary reported in AIR 1968 SC 1303 where Hedayatullah C.J. was virtually of the view that the satisfaction Of the detaining authority should be objective in that sense that their must he some material as the basis of the opinion of the detaining authority). 

 11. The principle finds its roots in the case of Ridge V. 13aldwin reported in 1964 AC 40 wherein Lord Reid quoted with approval the observation of Banks C'J in Rex V. Electricity Commissioner reported in (1924) I K 13 171 that a body of persons having legal authority to determine the questions affecting the rights of citizen had the duty to exercise the said power judicially. 

 12. In the case of l3egum Shorish kashmiri reported in 21 DLR SC I it has been observed that power is always coupled with a duty and that the power could only he exercised discharging the duty in accordance with law. 

 15. The learned Counsel for the petitioner further submitted that a criminal proceeding having been initiated earlier on the self-same subject matter against the detenu and there being no statements to the effect that there is possibility of immediate repetition of the same activities in the similar manner for which a criminal case has been started against the detenu, the High Court Division erred in affirming the order of detention of the detenu and has referred to a decision reported in the case M. Meera Rani V. Govt. of T.N. AIR 1989 SC 2027 reported in AIR 1989 SC 2027 and the cse of Salim Hasan Vs. Bangladesh reported in 45 DI,R (1993) 318. 

 16. In the case of N. Meera Rani V. State of Tamil Nadu and another reported in AIR 1989 SC 2027 one Nallathambi the husband of the petitioner was detained under the national Security Act. 1980 pursuant to the order dated 7.9.1998 made by the Collector and District 

 Magistrate, Maduri under section3(2) of the Act directing that the detenu be kept in custody in the Central prison, Maduri. Thereafter, the State Government by its order dated 25.10.1988 made under section 12(1) of the Act has confirmed the order of detention agreeing with the opinion of the Advisory Board constituted under the Act and directed that the detenu be kept in detention for a period of 12 months from the date of his detention. This preventive detention of the detenu was challenged in the High Court of Judicature at Madras under article 226 of Indian Constitution but the said High Court by its order dated 6.3.1989 dismissed the writ petition whereupon the petitioner has challenged the order of dismissal of the writ petition by special leave under Article 136 together with the another writ petition under Article 32 of the Indian Constitution. S. Verna J. as his lordship then was, held: "We may summarize and reiterate the settled principle. Subsisting custody of the detenu by-itself does not invalidate an order of his preventive detention and the decision must depend on the facts of the particular case; . preventive detention being necessary to prevent the detenu from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of the State or to the maintenance of public order etc. ordinarily it is not needed when the detenu is already in custody; the detaining authority must show its awareness to the fact of subsisting custody of the detenu and take that factor into account while making the order; but even so. if the detaining authority is reasonably satisfied on cogent material that there is likelihood of his release and in view of his antecedent activities which arc proximate in point of time he must be detained in order to prevent him from indulging in such prejudicial activities, the detention order can be validly made even in anticipation to operate on his release. This appears to us to he the correct legal position. 

 17. In he case of Salim hasan Vs. Bangladesh reported in 45 DIA (1993) 318 our  High Court Division considering certain decision has held that: 

 "Having considered those decision and after considering the submissions of the learned Advocates of the both the parties our view would he that in a detention matter the activities complained of may also provide for a criminal offence and punishable under the law and for that only there would exist no law for the same matter to be considered sufficient for a detention under the Special Powers Act when there are other specific independent grounds for detention, but where a criminal proceeding is essentially on the same subject matter and no other matter than the criminal proceeding, then the proceeding under the. normal law of the land would be allowed to be continued and the specific case would negative the necessity of any detention order except it could be shown on evidence or from records that proceeding would come to a fiasco because there is no possibility of any evidence to be produced in court in spite of attempts made by the prosecution for him to be punished eventually and there is a possibility of his immediately repeating the same activity in similar manner. A criminal proceeding thus would not bar a detention order but there are some limitations and we have spelt out those as aforesaid. It therefore depends on the facts and circumstances of each and there is no absolute formula which is to be followed." 18. It is true that there is a pending case against the detenu but as a general rule it cannot be said that a person already prosecuted in a case cannot be held in custody under the preventive detention so far the law cl' the !and is concerned. It is duty of the State to take both punitive and punitive measures for the self same case depending on the facts and circumstances of the case. A person can be prosecuted as a punitive measure for the selfsame offence already committed and could also be detained as a preventive measure for having been indulged himself in prejudicial activities enumerated in section 2(t) of the Special Powers Act. Although the detenu had been in custody since 04.12.2000 and was remanded in custody for 4 days in an specific criminal case and was enlarged on bail by the High Court Division in connection with the criminal case, the issuance of an order of detention dated 10.12.2000 would not be by itself invalid but the same will depend on the facts and circumstances of the case and the seriousness of the allegations warranting to prevent the detenu from indulging in activities prejudicial to the security of the State or to the maintenance of the public order etc. 

 19. In the case of Habiba Mahmud Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 45 DLR (AD) 89 the appellant's husband was arrested on August 20, 1991 in pursuance of an order of detention dated August 18, 1991 under section 3(1) (a) of the Special Powers Act, 1974 on the ground that he has been engaged in various anti-social and unlawful activities and resulting resentment and hatred against him in the minds of the public. For his oppressive and terrorist activities the detenu was suspended from the chairmanship of Kotowalipara Upazila. Nobody dares raise any objection against him as he organized an armed illegal bahini, his terrorizing activities is causing serious deterioration in law and order situation wherein it has been held that: "Pendency of a criminal case or cases involving petty offences, far removed from "prejudicial acts," as defined in the Act, can neither be a basis for reasonable apprehension or satisfaction for making an order of detention. But where the allegations are of serious nature the detaining authority may consider them and, despite the pendency of a criminal case, can make an order of detention if it is satisfied that the detenu is to be prevented, in view of his background, from indulging in prejudicial activities. Even after his acquittal in a criminal case a person may be detainer authority the Act. In that case, t to detaining authority will have to satisfy the Court that the necessity for a preventive measure survives, and that the acquittal was on technical ground, or on benefit of doubt or due to the witnesses' refusal to tell the truth for fear or reprisal from the accused or that fresh evidence dial has been discovered would have secured a conviction, if produced." 

 20. The words "allegations are of serious nature" has neither been spelt out nor explained in the aforesaid decision. The words 'serious' may mean and include to be grave, critical, important, approaching the critical or dangerous concerned with weighty matters. The said meanings are not exhaustive but narrative one. Serious in nature would always depend upon the facts and circumstances of a particular case. Allegations of murder abduction, rape or such other heinous and grievous offences may or may not be serious in nature usually for issuance of an order of preventive detention but in the facts and circumstances of the case the very allegation of each of the alleged offences may be serious in nature to justify an order of detention on which the detaining authority rests its satisfaction. The authority may, also in the absence of any legal evidence which usually is not forthcoming for obvious reasons or otherwise, having a cogent reason of suspicion in its mind as to the repetition or reasonable apprehension of repetition of the previous conduct which would he prejudicial activity or activities coming within the mischief of section 2th of the Special Powers Act, could detain the detenu in order to prevent him from indulging in prejudicial activities. 

 22. The High Court Division in the instant case has observed, inter alia, that the main allegations in the ground ()Noel-Him is that: "the detenu knowing fully well that Kaki Faroque is one of the top terrorists of the country included his name as Hazi Abdur Rashid as one of the artists of the group. As the attempt was made to take out of the country one of the top terrorists with a false identity, we are of the view that this act comes within the preview of prejudicial act as defined in section 2(1)(iii) and (v) of the Special Powers Act." 

 24. In the case of Barjahan Vs. State of West Bengal reported in AIR 1972 SC 2256 it has been held that the prosecution of the detenu in a criminal case would not debar an order of detention on the self same ground. The two jurisdictions are not coextensive nor they are alternative. The jurisdiction detaining a detenu could be availed of if no legal evidence is forthcoming but otherwise cogent enough to give rise to a suspicion in the mind or the authority that there is a reasonable likelihood of repetition of past conduct which would be prejudicial to the security of State or maintenance of public order and/ or maintenance of law-and order. 

 25. In the case of Kartik Chandra Gala Vs. State of West Bengal reported in AIR 1947 SC 2154 it was held that the power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised on reasonable suspicion and it is not a parallel proceeding to a criminal proceeding over the self same occurrence and it does not overlap with the prosecution. 

 26. In the case of Alijan Mian Vs. District Magistrate, Dhanbad reported in AIR 1988 SC 1130 the detenu threw Bomb on a cultural gathering and the detention was upheld even though the detenu was in jail custody on the date of passing of the order of detention because the detention order showed that the authority was alive to the fact yet was satisfied that if the detenu was enlarged on bail he would create problems of public order which necessitated his preventive detention. 

 27. The case of problem Lata Vs. M.L. Wadhamlac reported in AIR 1987 SC 2098 nullified the proposition that the detenu being already in custody in jail at the time of passing of the order of detention does not by itself initiate the detention lithe detaining authority is aware of this Baca but even then it is satisfied about the preventive detention. 

 28. From the above discussion, it can be safely concluded that in each of the above cases the conclusion reached rested on the fact of the particular case i.e. no uniform rule of law could be laid down for detaining a person in preventive detention but the ultimate decision of the authority would depend on the facts and circumstance's of each case. Thus the detenu being already in jail custody the mere possibility of his being enlarged on bail was not enough liar preventive detention unless there was suspicion or reasonable apprehension in the mind of the detaining authority that the detenu would indulge in activities prejudicial to the maintenance of public order etc. in case of release on bail. 

 29. Thus inspite of pendency of a criminal case over the selfsame allegations as have been detailed in the grounds of detention against the detenu and those allegations having the effect of trafficking criminals out of the Country or passing out information out of the country -or spreading the communal disturbance or disturbing communal harmony etc. and thereby creating an impression. apprehension or reasonable suspicion of likelihood of petition of the alleged offence in the mind of the detaining authority that the detenu may indulge in activities prejudicing the security of Bangladesh or maintenance of public order and the maintenance law and order of the Country etc. and such activity or activities being prima facie of serious  in nature the authority has the satisfaction requiring the detenu to he dealt with an order of detention for preventing him from indulging in prejudicial activities contemplated under section 2(f) of the Special Powers Act.
